suggestions.reason: Several assertions are pure section-name checks (Source Breakdown, Architecture Overview, Risks & Tradeoffs, Capability → Tech Mapping, Next Steps). The baseline contains content-equivalent material under different headings, so a grader applying the literal section name fails it while a substance-only grader would pass it. This is exactly where the skill differentiates — so the section-name assertions are doing useful discriminating work — but the eval would be more robust if each such assertion also named the substantive requirement (e.g., 'a section that maps every capability to implementing technology'), so partial-credit ambiguity is removed and the assertion can't be gamed by a heading alone.

No assertion checks technical quality/correctness of the recommendations. The baseline (no skill) is arguably technically richer (diagrams, end-to-end flows, SLOs, phased roadmap) yet scores far lower purely on structure/process compliance. If the eval's intent is to reward the skill's value, that's correct here; but adding at least one substance assertion (e.g., 'ledger is double-entry and reconciled against the gateway') would confirm the skill doesn't win on format alone.

eval_feedback.overall: Applied the identical 23 assertions honestly. The baseline is a strong architecture document but fails the prescribed-structure and skill-integration assertions; it passes only the substance/coverage assertions that are heading-agnostic.
